column1: What is the principle of compositionality (truth-functionality) in propositional logic?
column2: The truth value of a compound formula depends exclusively on the truth values of its constituent atomic propositions and the semantics of the connectives binding them, making semantic evaluation reducible to finite computation.

column1: Define the three canonical semantic classifications of propositional formulas.
column2: Tautology: true under every assignment (e.g., $p \lor \neg p$). Contradiction: false under every assignment (e.g., $p \land \neg p$). Contingent: true under some assignments, false under others.

column1: Distinguish semantic entailment ($\models$) from syntactic derivability ($\vdash$) in proof theory.
column2: $\Gamma \models \varphi$ means every valuation satisfying $\Gamma$ also satisfies $\varphi$ (truth-table/model-based). $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ means $\varphi$ can be derived from $\Gamma$ via a finite sequence of syntactic inference rules.

column1: State the Soundness and Completeness theorems for propositional/first-order logic.
column2: Soundness: if $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ then $\Gamma \models \varphi$ (derivability never overreaches truth). Completeness: if $\Gamma \models \varphi$ then $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ (every semantic truth is formally derivable). Together they make $\vdash$ and $\models$ coextensive.

column1: What distinguishes Hilbert-style proof systems from other propositional proof architectures?
column2: Hilbert-style systems minimize the number of inference rules, relying almost entirely on a rich set of logical axioms plus typically only modus ponens, optimizing for metatheoretical elegance over practical derivation ease.

column1: What are the three ingredients of a first-order language's non-logical signature?
column2: Constant symbols (nullary terms naming individuals), function symbols (fixed arity, build compound terms), and predicate/relation symbols (fixed arity, express properties/relations among individuals).

column1: What do the universal ($\forall$) and existential ($\exists$) quantifiers add to propositional logic's expressive power?
column2: They allow claims ranging over all ($\forall$) or at least one ($\exists$) element of a domain, enabling statements about objects and relationships that propositional logic—lacking terms and quantification—cannot express.

Every first-order formula derivable from axioms $\Gamma$ via formal deduction is true in every model of $\Gamma$, and conversely every semantically valid consequence of $\Gamma$ admits a finite formal proof.

column1: State the Compactness Theorem and give one key application.
column2: If every finite subset of a first-order theory $T$ has a model, then $T$ itself has a model. Application: constructing non-standard models of arithmetic containing infinite integers.

column1: State the Downward and Upward Löwenheim–Skolem Theorems.
column2: Downward: a countable first-order theory with an infinite model has a countable model. Upward: any infinite model of a theory can be extended to a model of arbitrarily larger cardinality. Together they show first-order logic cannot categorically fix infinite cardinalities.

column1: Define the components of a deterministic Turing machine tuple.
column2: $M = (Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, q_{accept}, q_{reject})$: $Q$ finite states, $\Sigma$ input alphabet, $\Gamma \supseteq \Sigma$ tape alphabet (includes blank $\sqcup$), $\delta$ transition function, $q_0$ start state, and distinct accept/reject halting states.

column1: What is the core mechanism Gödel used to prove the First Incompleteness Theorem, and what is its consequence?
column2: Arithmetic self-reference via Gödel numbering: the formal system (e.g., Peano Arithmetic) can encode statements about its own provability, yielding a true but unprovable self-referential sentence. Consequence: any sufficiently expressive consistent formal system is incomplete—there exist true statements it cannot prove.
